1:
The chapter opens with the double name. Gill notes only that it was lately given him by his father; Clarke, that it had become a surname from the incident of the altar; and Ellicott sets it among the Scriptural characters who carry two names. Henry attends to the hour and the ground. He rose early, as one whose heart was upon his business and afraid of losing time; now that he is sure God is with him he is impatient of delay, and faith in God's promises must not slacken but rather quicken our endeavours. He pitched near a famous well so his army might not want water, and gained the higher ground, the enemy lying beneath him in the valley. Ellicott presses the point through the preposition: the word rendered beside is rather above, since it would have been dangerous to encamp on the plain.

Both the well and the hill draw comment. The name of the spring means trembling, and Ellicott takes it for an allusion to the timidity of the people the next verses describe, so that it is used here by anticipation; Clarke reaches the same root, which signifies to shake through fear, but refers it forward to the panic that seized the Midianite host at this place. Ellicott adds that the name occurs here only, and that since the camp lay on Gilboa it must be the abundant spring at the foot of the hill now called the spring of Goliath, from a mistaken legend that the giant died there. Of the hill he is more cautious. The only Moreh known from elsewhere is at Shechem, five and twenty miles south, so the word must here stand for Little Hermon, the Latin turning it into a lofty hill, perhaps to avoid a supposed difficulty. Since Moreh means archer, Ellicott suggests Little Hermon may have been the Archer's Hill, from the bowmen of the Amalekites.

Then the army is cut down, and Henry reads the reduction as a provision that the praise be reserved to God. Thirty-two thousand was a small force beside what Midian had brought into the field, and their leader was ready to think them too few when God told him they were too many. Henry gives three reasons. God would show that when he employs suitable instruments he does not need them, being not indebted to them for their service, but they to him for their employment. He would shame those who had tamely submitted to Midian for the disproportion of numbers, since they now saw that had they made sure of God's favour, one of them might have chased a thousand. And he would exclude boasting, which is the reason given in the text itself — for my own hand hath saved me is a word that must never come out of the mouth of such as shall be saved, and he that glories must glory in the Lord. The first winnowing dismissed the fearful, and Henry pauses on the law providing for such a proclamation, which their leader may have thought applied only to wars for enlarging their coast, not to a necessary defence, so he would not have proclaimed it unbidden. Cowards would be as likely as any to take the honour from God after a victory, and so God would not do them the honour of employing them. One would have thought scarcely an Israelite would own himself fearful under such a leader, yet more than two parts in three filed off. Some think the long oppression had broken their spirits; Henry thinks it likelier that consciousness of their own guilt had taken away their courage, since sin stared them in the face and therefore they durst not look death in the face. Faint-hearted people are not fit to be employed for God, and among those enlisted under Christ's banner there are more such than we think.
2:
Keil sets the arithmetic out: the Israelite force stood at thirty-two thousand and Midian with its allies at about a hundred and thirty-five thousand, so the disproportion was already great when the Lord called the smaller number too many, the Hebrew being comparative. Ellicott says this must have put Gideon's faith to a severe trial, and Gill observes the odds were heavy against him before any reduction at all. Clarke gives the reason from the other end: had a numerous host been led up, the excellence of the power that discomfited the enemy might have seemed of man and not of God, whereas the manner of the whole made both nations see that the thing was of God — inspiring the one with confidence and the other with fear.

The proclamation that follows is exactly the law's, and Ellicott notes what that law rests on: cowardice is contagious, so timid men are a direct danger. He cites the rule kept by Judas Maccabaeus and by Epaminondas before Leuctra, with the Roman remark that even where there are many legions it is always the few that win. Gill thinks Gideon would not have made the proclamation unbidden, and may have taken the law to concern wars of conquest only. Two phrases give trouble. The word rendered depart early occurs only here: the Chaldee explains it as in the morning, another renders it hastily, like a bird, and Keil connects it with an Arabic root meaning to twist round, hence to slink away by by-paths — Ellicott hears contempt in it. Harder is the phrase from mount Gilead, since Gilead lies across Jordan and the camp lay near Gilboa. Clarke reports the suggestion of two Gileads, and the conjecture that the text should read Gilboa, which no manuscript countenances; he prefers the solution that many eastern Manassites from Gilead were in the army, more afraid of their Midianite neighbours than the western tribes, so the sense is, whosoever from Gilead is fearful, let him go home. Ellicott adds that Gilead was a son of Abiezer, so the name may have been a rallying-cry of Manasseh, the phrase meaning let him leave that camp. Twenty-two thousand went, and Clarke is astonished that so many would fight neither for God nor for their country — though he allows that slavery debases the mind, and that if the armies of Europe had the same address from their generals, an equal proportion would go home. Ellicott thinks many of them joined the pursuit later.

The water test divides them sharply. Ellicott reports Josephus, who has the men brought down in the noon heat and judges those who flung themselves down the braver and the hasty lappers the cowards, Theodoret making the divine aid appear in the choosing of the most timid; but Ellicott thinks greater self-control is shown by stooping and drinking from the hand than by falling at full length. He passes on the rabbinic notion that those who knelt were secret idolaters who had bowed to Baal. Gill lays both readings side by side without deciding, noting that Ben Gersom took the kneelers for slothful and the lappers for courageous, which agrees with the earlier dismissal. Keil is firm that the three hundred were not the cowardly or indolent, and explains the action as taking water in the hollow of the hand and lapping it in. Clarke adds that the verb reproduces the very sound a dog makes in drinking. On the provisions Ellicott prefers the ancient versions, which make the three hundred take the victuals and trumpets of the rest: supplies would be scarce near so vast a host, and but for this verse we might wonder how each got a horn. Gill concludes that with food in one hand and a trumpet in the other they were unarmed, so the salvation would most clearly appear to be the Lord's.
9:
Henry sees the point at once: the army being cut to a handful, its captain must fight by faith or not at all, and so God provides recruits for his faith instead of his forces. He is given a word of command to warrant an action that otherwise looked rash, and a word of promise to assure him of a success that looked improbable; and it came the same night, when he may be supposed full of care — divine consolations are given to believers not only strongly but seasonably. Clarke reads the promise as a thing already done — I have determined it, and it is as sure as if accomplished — and Keil says the same of the Hebrew tense, which denotes a purpose already formed. Then he is made his own spy. God knows the infirmities of his people, Henry says, and what great encouragement they may take from a small matter, and so, knowing what would be said in that quarter of the camp, he sends him to hear it. Phurah goes as one he could confide in and a witness besides, that the word might be established out of the mouth of two — two being better than one, and a little help better than none.

Ellicott measures the nerve this took against a more famous three hundred: the courage went beyond Thermopylae, since these were to attack in the open plain, not hold a pass. What Gideon was to hear he identifies as the omen the Jews called the daughter of a voice — sometimes a voice from heaven, sometimes an echo, sometimes the first chance words a man hears after being bidden to watch for them. It ranked as one of four modes of divine direction, with prophets, dreams and Urim, though lowest of the four. Gill observes that though it was the dead of night, something would be heard — a clear proof, he thinks, of God's foreknowledge. Clarke supposes the multitude, having come merely for plunder, was unarmed but kept guards on the outside as caravans do; Ellicott renders the word for them literally as ranks by five and thinks it means sentries. Henry notes the sight that met them: men like grasshoppers for multitude, though they proved no better than grasshoppers for courage.

The cake has been much worked over. Ellicott reports that the noun occurs nowhere else and the rabbinic derivations yield no sense, while the Chaldee, the Greek, the Latin and Josephus all make it a cake baked on coals, as the desert Arabs still bake dough in ashes. That it was barley he thinks the point of the symbol, Josephus adding that men can hardly eat such bread. The raids had reduced Israel to living on it, and if the Midianites were used to taunting Gideon's people as eaters of barley bread, as later Bedouins do, the application would be the more natural — Josephus has the soldier say that as barley is the vilest seed, so Israel was the vilest people of Asia. Henry is blunter about the dream, calling it foolish, as our dreams generally are, since in the multitude of them there are many vanities; the interpretation he calls far-fetched. Yet he grants how apt the resemblance turns out — a man who had threshed corn and made cakes fitly figured by a cake, his force as inconsiderable as a cake of a little flour, and as unlikely to overthrow that army as a cake to overturn a tent. But after all, he asks, do not interpretations belong to God? Clarke says flatly that both dream and interpretation were inspired, to increase one man's confidence and appal his enemies. Gill dwells on the word for the interpretation, which means a breaking: the dream was like something sealed, its reading like a nut whose kernel cannot be got at till the shell is broken.
16:
Henry sets the attack beside Abraham's rescue of Lot: the numbers nearly the same, both leaders divided their forces, both struck by night, both conquered under great disadvantage — Gideon a son of Abraham by descent, as the Midianites also were through Keturah, but an heir of his faith besides. Gill gives the practical reason for three companies of a hundred: partly to make a show of an army with right and left wing, partly to fall on the camp at different points. Ellicott notes that dividing an attacking force was a common stratagem, used by Saul against Ammon and by David against Absalom; and he sees the point of the horns, since hearing three hundred the Midianites would suppose three hundred companies were upon them. Clarke draws a lesson from the arrangements: though the victory was to be from the Lord, prudential means were still used — had they not been, it is not likely God would have delivered the enemy up, for even in working a miracle he will have natural means employed, as when a man was told to dip in Jordan or wash in Siloam.

The equipment is described closely. Ellicott identifies the vessels as earthenware jars, the word being cognate with our cask, so the Latin rendering by flagons is mistaken; the lamps he takes for firebrands or torches rather than lamps proper. His best illustration is a modern one: the police officer of Cairo carried at night a torch which burns without flame once lit, blazing up when waved, and answering the purpose of a dark lantern, its burning end concealed in a small pot when light was not wanted. Henry sees in the outfit a design to make the rout not only fatal but shameful. A trumpet in the right hand and a pitcher with a torch in the left is to jest at an enemy, going out as against children rather than soldiers, so that the daughter of Zion laughs them to scorn. On the order to watch him, Ellicott says he showed all three hundred what he wished done at the signal, which his own hundred would give; Henry hears the word of command the captain of our salvation gives his soldiers, having left us an example with a charge to follow it.

The hour was chosen as carefully as the gear. Keil places the beginning of the middle watch at midnight, and Ellicott explains that the Jews divided the night into three watches, the four-watch reckoning being later borrowed from the Romans, so the attack fell soon after ten, when the host would be in its first sleep; the words about the watch being newly set mean the assault came while the guard was changing. Henry adds that in the night all frights are most frightful, and that fewness favoured secrecy, so small a party reaching the camp unnoticed. He sets out three instruments of terror: a great noise, each man blowing his horn and dashing his pitcher, probably against his neighbour's so that both broke together — itself a figure of what followed when the Midianites killed one another; a great blaze, the torches hid like a candle under a bushel and then flashing through the camp like lightning, perhaps firing the outer tents; and a great shout. The cry itself is disputed. Henry would read it for the Lord and for Gideon, the word sword not standing in the Hebrew here, and thinks it borrowed from the dream, the name that had proved a terror being turned against them but with the divine name prefixed, without which his own was an insignificant cypher. Clarke holds the word genuine, absent here but present in the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic and in eight collated manuscripts; Ellicott thinks it better omitted, the phrase being literally for Jehovah and for Gideon, like the watchword Cyrus gave his soldiers.
20:
Clarke asks the reader to picture it: in a dark night, the sudden glare of three hundred torches on the half-awakened eyes of the enemy, with the clangour of three hundred trumpets mingled with the thundering shout. Ellicott observes that the men were by that arrangement comparatively defenceless, a horn in one hand and a brand in the other, though a shield might hang on the left arm and a sword be girded on the thigh. Startled from sleep in a camp imperfectly protected, the Midianites would see blazing lights on every side and hear horns and a war-cry from every quarter; and the first thought to rise would be that treachery was at work among the motley elements of the camp itself. The result was a wild panic like that which seized the Persians at Plataea — and even a well-disciplined camp, Ellicott adds, is liable to such outbursts, as the Ten Thousand were, whose commander next morning proclaimed a reward for whoever would say who had let the ass loose, a joke afterwards used to shame soldiers out of groundless alarms. Keil supplies the detail that gave the illusion its force: the three hundred stood without moving, so the enemy necessarily supposed a numerous army was advancing behind the torch-bearers.

Ellicott collects the parallels. One ancient writer on the art of war records a commander attacking Heraea who set his trumpeters apart to sound a charge from many quarters, so that the townsmen, thinking the region crowded with enemies, abandoned it. Hannibal once escaped Fabius Maximus by tying torches to the heads of cattle, and an Arab chief of the eighteenth century used trumpets in exactly this manner, with the same success. Clarke's collection runs the other way, into allegory. Origen made the three hundred types of the preachers of the gospel, their trumpets the preaching of Christ crucified, their torches the conduct of righteous men; and some verses against Marcion turn them into horsemen and find in the number the mystery of the cross, since the Greek letter standing for three hundred is itself the shape of a cross. Clarke prints the verses, then gives his verdict: we see here what abstruse meanings a strong imagination, assisted by a little piety, may extract from what was never intended as a mystery.

Why the three hundred did not charge is answered plainly. Gill says they stood to see the salvation of God, and had they gone in could have done nothing, having no weapons; but their standing increased the terror, since the enemy might suppose they stood either to light a large army in behind them or to light the forces already among them while these destroyed them — the latter seeming what possessed them, since they fell to killing their fellows. They kept blowing to increase the fright, and stood as torch-bearers to light the Midianites in destroying one another. Clarke reads it the same way: each company kept its station and sounded on, and the enemy, believing these the trumpets of a numerous army already within the camp, turned their swords against every man they met while trying to escape. No stratagem, he says, was ever better imagined, better executed, or more completely successful. Keil renders the outcry as anguish, and the next verb as carrying off — the enemy hurrying away tents and herds. Ellicott takes the running and crying as men casting about to learn what the blast meant, their cries the wail of despair or confused words of command; and he sets the mutual slaughter beside the Ammonites and Moabites destroying each other before Jehoshaphat. Of the places named he can say little: the house of the acacia, from trees still abundant there; the meadow of the dance, native place of Elisha; and a name meaning famous, whose site is unknown. Clarke observes that most occur nowhere else in Scripture.
23:
The men who come in for the pursuit are those who had been sent home. Keil says so plainly: those of Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh had been dismissed before the battle and were on their way back, and could be recalled quickly; the omission of Zebulun he puts down to brevity. Clarke and Ellicott agree, Ellicott adding that Naphtali and Asher would chase the fugitives northward and Manasseh those who made for the lower fords. Henry is sharper. Those afraid to fight now took heart when the worst was over, and were ready enough to divide the spoil though backward to make the onset; yet he distinguishes them from the hired troops of a later reign who went home in a rage, for these waited for an opportunity of service, though denied the honour of forcing the lines.

The Ephraimites were summoned separately, and Ellicott notices the timing: their leader had not ventured to call on these haughty clansmen until the victory was assured. What they were to take is disputed only in detail. Ellicott glosses the phrase as intercepting the flight, and takes the waters for marshes formed by streams running from the Ephraim hills down to the Jordan; Keil, that since they are named before the Jordan and distinguished from it, they must be the brooks the flying men would have to cross before reaching the river. Gill puts it simply: the point was to get the fords first. Where Beth-barah lay nobody can say. Keil reports that even Eusebius could give nothing definite, and Ellicott renders the name house of the waste, against Jerome's house of the well; Clarke, more confidently, takes it for the place where Israel forded Jordan under Joshua. Henry sees the trap closing: they took the waters, posting themselves along the river side, so that those fleeing from their pursuers fell into the hands of the men waiting to intercept them — here were fear, and the pit, and the snare. Now that the enemy had begun to fall, he adds, it was easy to say, Down with them.

The two princes have names that have interested everyone. Gill gives them as raven and wolf, and thinks them either nicknames fastened on them for cruelty or titles taken to make themselves feared. Clarke enlarges the point: in all ancient nations generals took names from birds and beasts, the Romans having their jackdaws, crows and eagles, and we ourselves our Crows, Wolfs, Lyons and Hawkes. Ellicott is more cautious, holding such names common among nomads and no mark of scorn. Where the two were caught became their memorial. Clarke has one taking shelter in the cavern of a rock and the other in the vat of a winepress, both afterwards called by their names; Henry gives the point an edge — the places of their shelter were made the places of their slaughter, and the man who destroyed them had himself, for fear of them, lately hidden his corn by a winepress. Ellicott renders the first site as the raven's rock, mentioned again only once, in a prophet recalling the slaughter of Midian there. Of the heads carried to Gideon Clarke observes that among barbarous nations the head of a conquered chief was commonly brought to the conqueror, as Pompey's to Caesar, and that for the credit of human nature it is a pity such things were ever done. Ellicott points out that the closing notice is given by anticipation, the crossing of the Jordan not being related till the next chapter, and that the rout left its mark on the national memory, the prophets needing only to speak of the day of Midian. Henry closes with a wish: that where help is needed it were as willingly given as here, and that when a good work is begun we were as ready to welcome fellow-labourers as we often are to hinder one another.
